To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
primate ES cell grafts contain neurons that resemble the normal DA phenotype and that these cells have the ability to form connections with the host brain.

(1) ES cell‐derived dopamine neurons are able to integrate into the rat brain, (2) they express markers of midbrain dopamine neurons and (3) they innervate DARPR‐32 expressing neurons within the striatum.

(1) ES‐derived graft cells express regional transcription factors that are normally present in striatal neurons; (2) ES‐derived TH neurons express markers that define the DA phenotype; (3) ES‐derived DA neurons are capable of forming synapses with striatal neurons; and (4) ES‐derived striatopallidal and striatostriatal projections are preferentially targeted to DARPP‐32 expressing neurons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel stem cell therapy for Parkinson's Disease.
the use of primate embryonic stem cells for the development of cell replacement therapies for Parkinson's disease.
the generation of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) for use in cell replacement strategies for Parkinson's disease (PD) and other neurodegenerative diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ES cell‐derived DA neurons have the same phenotype and functional capacity of their fetal counterparts, at least within this experimental paradigm.
the ES cell grafts are functional in the rat model of Parkinson's disease, and that this is not a function of the cell source, but rather a function of the graft composition.
primate ES cells can be differentiated into DA‐containing neurons in vitro and these cells have the capacity to integrate into the host brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the grafts derived from the 6 weeks differentiated ES cells have a higher proportion of TH neurons and that these cells are able to form connections with the DARPP‐32 neurons in the host striatum.
the use of primate ES cells as a source of DA neurons for transplantation in Parkinson's disease is feasible, and may be a promising approach for the future treatment of this disease.
primate ES‐cell‐derived neurons are able to survive and integrate in the host brain and to restore motor functions in a rodent model of Parkinson's disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of primate ES cells to generate dopamine neurons is a viable approach for the generation of a cell‐based therapy for Parkinson's Disease.
primate ES cells can be differentiated in vitro to produce a heterogeneous mixture of DA neurons and striatal progenitors.
primate ES cells can be differentiated into DA neurons with a high degree of phenotypic fidelity and functional capacity.
